summary: Revisits the advice of RFC 3177 that end sites get /48 blocks of IPv6 space, and obsoletes that recommendation, leaving the exact choice to the operational community. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary:
RFC 6177 replaces an earlier advice that every organisation receiving IPv6 address space should get a block of /48 size. That size was fixed for everybody, from a home network to a large company, and it wasted a lot of address space.

The document does not say what size to use instead. It says what an address policy has to achieve: an organisation must be able to get enough space for several subnetworks and for growth over many years, and it must never be pushed into conserving addresses by tricks such as address translation.

questions: how big an ipv6 prefix for end sites
what prefix size should an ipv6 end site get
is a /56 enough for a home network
should i assign a /128 to an end site
subtitle: Why the IETF stopped prescribing one fixed IPv6 prefix size for every end site.

tldr.problem: RFC 3177 recommended that every end site receive a /48 block of IPv6 address space. Regional registries adopted that advice, then found it wasteful, because a home network and a large company received the same amount of space.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6177 withdraws the /48 default and lists what an address policy should take into account instead. It keeps the underlying principle, that an end site must be able to get enough space for several subnets and for growth over years, and leaves the exact size to the operational community.
tldr.outcome: The document is Best Current Practice 157 and obsoletes RFC 3177. Registries moved to smaller defaults such as /56, and the document keeps the strong prohibition on handing out a single /128 to a site.

today: RFC 6177 is Best Current Practice 157, published in March 2011. It obsoleted RFC 3177, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The document leaves the exact assignment size to the operational community and instead sets out the properties any policy has to satisfy.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Several considerations factor into address assignment policies. For the long-term health and scalability of the public routing infrastructure, it is important that addresses aggregate well. Giving out an excessive amount of address space could result in premature depletion of the address space. This document focuses on the narrower question of what is an appropriate IPv6 address assignment size for end sites, that is, what size is appropriate when end sites request address space from ISPs.

RFC 3177 called for a default end site assignment size of /48. The Regional Internet Registries then developed and adopted policies consistent with that recommendation. In 2005 they began discussing assignment policy again, and since then APNIC, ARIN and RIPE have revised end site policy to encourage the assignment of smaller, /56, blocks.

This document obsoletes RFC 3177 and updates its recommendations in three ways. It is no longer recommended that /128s be given out, although there may be cases where assigning only a single address can be justified, since a site by definition implies multiple subnets and multiple devices. RFC 3177 specifically recommended prefix lengths of /48, /64 and /128, and naming a small number of fixed boundaries raised concerns that implementations and operational practices might become hard-coded to recognise only those boundaries, which the document calls a return to classful addressing; the intention has always been that there be no hard-coded boundaries and that CIDR continues to apply to all bits of the routing prefixes. Third, the document moves away from a single default assignment size, because end sites come in different shapes and sizes and a one-size-fits-all approach is not necessary or appropriate.

The document does reaffirm an important assumption behind RFC 3177: end sites must always be able to obtain a reasonable amount of address space for their actual and planned usage, and over time ranges specified in years rather than just months. In practice that means at least one /64, and in most cases significantly more. One situation that must be avoided is an end site feeling compelled to use IPv6-to-IPv6 Network Address Translation or other burdensome address conservation techniques because it could not get sufficient address space.
sections.plainLanguage:
The old advice gave every organisation the same amount of address space. That was wasteful for a small network and unhelpful for a large one, so the registries started handing out smaller blocks.

Three things changed. A single address on its own is no longer recommended, because a site is more than one device. Naming a few fixed sizes as good defaults is no longer recommended, because that leads to software that only understands those sizes. And there is no longer a single recommended size for everybody.

sections.title: Why /48 Was Recommended
sections.content:
Three concerns drove the original /48 recommendation. The first was to ensure that end sites could easily obtain sufficient address space without having to jump through hoops to do so. In IPv4, a typical home user is given a single public IP address, and getting any more than one address is often difficult or impossible unless one is willing to pay a significantly increased fee for what is often considered a higher grade of service. An important goal in IPv6 was to change the default and minimal end site assignment from a single address to multiple networks, and to ensure that end sites could easily obtain address space.

The second motivation was to simplify the management of an end site's addressing plan in the presence of renumbering, such as when switching ISPs. In IPv6 a site may use multiple prefixes at once, including public prefixes from ISPs and Unique Local Addresses. Where there are multiple prefixes, it is less complex to manage a numbering plan if the same subnet numbering plan works for all of them, so that the subnet portion of those prefixes is identical for all assigned addresses. Renumbering from a larger set of subnet bits into a smaller set is often painful, because it can require making changes to the network itself, such as collapsing subnets. Similar arguments apply to managing the reverse ip6.arpa tree in DNS, which is simplified when all links are numbered with the same subnet identifiers.

The third motivation was to better support network growth common at many sites. In IPv4 it is usually difficult or impossible to obtain public address space for more than a few months of projected growth, so even slow growth over several years can lead to a need to renumber into a larger address block. With IPv6's vast address space, end sites can be given more space than in IPv4 to support expected growth over multi-year periods.

The /48 recommendation simplifies address space management for end sites, but it has also been widely criticised as wasteful. A large business with thousands of employees would by default receive the same amount of address space as a home user, who typically has a single or small number of LANs and a small number of devices, dozens or less. While it seems likely that the size of a typical home network will grow over the next few decades, it is hard to argue that home sites will make use of 65K subnets within the foreseeable future. It might be tempting to give home sites a single /64, since that is already significantly more address space than today's IPv4 practice, but that precludes the expectation that even home sites will grow to support multiple subnets. The document therefore still recommends giving home sites significantly more than a single /64, while not recommending that every home site be given a /48 either.

Changing the default assignment from a /48 to a /56 for the vast majority of end sites, home sites among them, would save up to 8 bits and reduce total projected address consumption by up to 8 bits, or two orders of magnitude. The exact saving depends on the relative number of home users compared with larger sites. The goals of RFC 3177 can easily be met by giving home users a default assignment of less than /48, such as a /56.
sections.plainLanguage:
The /48 recommendation was sensible when it was written. It let a site get more space without arguing, made renumbering easier because the subnet part of the address stayed the same, and left room to grow for years.

What it did not do was match the amount of space to the site. A home network with a few dozen devices does not need room for 65K subnets, and giving it that much wastes address space that the whole internet has to carry in routing tables.

sections.title: Other RFC 3177 Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 3177 suggested that some multihoming approaches, such as the Generalized Structure Element, might benefit from having a fixed /48 boundary. This no longer appears to be a consideration.

RFC 3177 also argued that a single default assignment size reduced the need for customers to justify the usage of existing address space in order to get a little more, and reduced the need for ISPs to evaluate such requests. Given the large amount of address space in IPv6, there is plenty of space to grant end sites enough to be consistent with reasonable growth projections over multi-year time frames, so it remains highly desirable to provide end sites with enough space, on both initial and subsequent assignments, to last several years. Fortunately this goal can be achieved in a number of ways and does not require that all end sites receive the same default size assignment.
sections.plainLanguage: The old document also hoped that a fixed size would spare everyone the need to ask for more space later. That goal still holds, but it no longer requires one fixed size, because IPv6 has enough address space to be generous without giving every site the same amount.

sections.title: Impact on IPv6 Standards
sections.content:
RFC 3056 describes a way of generating IPv6 addresses from an existing public IPv4 address. It defines an address format in which the first 48 bits concatenate a well-known prefix with a globally unique public IPv4 address, and the SLA ID field is assumed to be 16 bits, consistent with a 16-bit subnet identifier field. To make the move from the numbering scheme of RFC 3056 to one based on a prefix obtained from an ISP easier, an end site is advised to number out of the rightmost bits first, using the leftmost bits only if the size of the site made that necessary. Similar considerations apply to other documents that allow for a subnet identifier of 16 bits, including the specification of Unique Local Addresses.

Some IPv6 multicast address assignment schemes embed a unicast IPv6 prefix into the multicast address itself. Such documents do not assume a particular size for the subnet identifier, but do assume that the IPv6 prefix is a /64, so the relative size of the subnet identifier has no direct impact on multicast address schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the recommended size does not break the standards that depend on it. Documents that build IPv6 addresses from IPv4 ones, and documents that embed a unicast prefix in a multicast address, either leave room to work or assume a /64 prefix, so the subnet identifier size makes no difference to them.

sections.title: Summary
sections.content:
The exact choice of how much address space to assign end sites is an issue for the operational community. The recommendation in RFC 3177 to assign /48s as a default is not a requirement of the IPv6 architecture: anything of length /64 or shorter works from a standards perspective. There are important operational considerations as well, some of which matter if users are to share in the key benefit of IPv6, which is expanding the usable address space of the internet. The IETF recommends that any policy on IPv6 address assignment to end sites take into consideration the following.

  • It should be easy for an end site to obtain address space to number multiple subnets, a block larger than a single /64, and to support reasonable growth projections over long time periods, such as a decade or more.
  • The default assignment size should take into consideration the likelihood that an end site will have need for multiple subnets in the future, and avoid the IPv4 practice of having frequent and continual justification for obtaining small amounts of additional space.
  • Although a /64 can in theory address an almost unlimited number of devices, sites should be given sufficient address space to be able to lay out subnets as appropriate, and not be forced to use address conservation techniques such as bridging. Whether or not bridging is an appropriate choice is an end site matter.
  • Assigning a longer prefix to an end site, compared with the existing prefixes it already has, is likely to increase operational costs and complexity for the end site, with insufficient benefit to anyone.
  • The operational considerations of managing and delegating the reverse DNS tree under ip6.arpa on nibble versus non-nibble boundaries should be given adequate consideration.
sections.plainLanguage: Five points summarise the advice. Give a site enough space for several subnets and for growth over a decade or more. Size the default for what the site will probably need, so nobody has to keep asking for a little more. Do not force a site to conserve addresses, for instance by bridging, just because it was given only one subnet's worth. Changing to a longer prefix than the site already uses costs the site work for little gain. And think about how the reverse DNS tree under ip6.arpa will be managed before picking a boundary.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document has no known security implications. It deals with how much address space an organisation is given, and not with the addresses themselves or with the traffic that uses them.
sections.plainLanguage: The document has nothing to say about security, because changing the size of an address block does not change who can reach whom.

items.text: A site should be able to obtain address space to number multiple subnets and to support growth over a decade or more.

items.title: No repeated justification
items.text: The default size should reflect the likelihood of needing several subnets, rather than the IPv4 practice of asking again for a little more space.

items.title: Space to lay out subnets
items.text: Although a /64 can address an almost unlimited number of devices, sites should have enough space to lay out subnets and not be forced into address conservation techniques such as bridging.

items.title: Mind the cost of a longer prefix
items.text: Assigning a longer prefix than the site already has is likely to increase operational costs and complexity, with insufficient benefit to anyone.
